title: Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI
pitch: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you.
about_excerpt: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you. Like Comment Story Updates AI to AI data transfer Lora adapter for better MCP use List of all WebMCP tool on the website Multi-step task can be compressed to single webmcp call Agent using actual webMCP calls to use tools from the website Inspiration I run mentria.ai, an extensible toolbox: 34 tools, 8 games, user-installable extensions and an AI-learning feed, all running in the browser, including language models of up to 27B parameters executing on the visitor's own GPU through WebGPU (smaller models cover low-end devices). The core of the site never sends your data anywhere. A few features, like the comms chat or the peer swarm for model downloads, talk to a server or to other people, and only when you turn them on. Every tool already registered its abilities on an in-page "capability bus" so my on-device model could operate them. WebMCP is a browser API that lets a web page publish its functions as tools that any AI agent (a browser's assistant, an in-app browser, an extension) can discover and call. It is the same idea I had built for my own model, now as a standard that any agent understands. So the question became: what happens when outside agents get the same doors my local model already uses, and what can the local model do for them? What it does One bridge, whole site agent-ready. mentria-webmcp.js registers every AI-safe capability with document.modelContext , picks up tools that appear later, and marks the read-only ones so agents know what is safe to call. Because the bus announces across tabs, an agent sitting on the notes page can also spin the decision wheel, start a timer or create a story in Story Studio if those tabs are open, all from where it is. Agents operate the real UI. Spin the decision wheel and it visibly spins in your tab; ask for a QR code and it renders in the tool; start a timer and the tab title counts down. An on-page "Agent activity" panel lists every call an agent makes with its arguments and result, so nothing happens out of sight. The person watches, interrupts, or takes over at any point. The on-device model as a privacy layer. Capabilities that read private data are never exposed to agents. Instead the site exposes a tool backed by the model running on your device: an outside agent that needs something from your notes calls notes__summarize_private , the local model reads the notes, and only the summary goes back. local_ai__ask generalizes it, so any agent can hand any prompt to the model on your GPU, and an on-page panel streams the local answer so you always see what your model said. The agent gets what it needs; the data never leaves. Extensible by anyone. Extensions are single HTML files that register capabilities on the same bus. The bundled Story Studio, Unit Converter and Dice Roller installed from the Extensions page (/tools/extensions/) show up to agents automatically, and anyone can add a tool without touching this repo. The same tools, from the inside. The site's own agent at /tools/console/ is a 27B model in a browser tab, fine-tuned for tool calling with a LoRA trained on our own machines. Ask it to "create a story from @notes.1" and it reads my private note, makes one call, and a titled five-slide story appears in the studio. The homepage prompt answers from the same local model. How we built it Every capability is described once on the bus (name, description, JSON schema, ai and read-only flags), and one bridge file turns those descriptions into WebMCP tool registrations. It is feature-detected, so browsers without WebMCP pay nothing, and an origin-trial token is served so testing needs no flags. The site is Eleventy plus plain JavaScript, no bundler, hosted as static files; models are downloaded once from our mirror and cached on the device. The tool-call LoRA was trained in about fifteen minutes on our in-house pipeline and hot-swaps at runtime. Only one model instance runs at a time: tabs coordinate over a broadcast channel, so a tab that already holds the model answers on behalf of the others instead of loading a second copy. The on-device agent also tests the site: a console__test capability lets any agent commission a QA run of a tool, and the model reports what worked, what was awkward and what broke. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is per-document. An agent on one page could not see the tools of another, so I built a cross-tab announce layer on the bus. Now one page exposes the tools of every open tab. Agents hit bugs people never do. Chrome throttles animation frames in background tabs, so an agent working in one could wait forever on an animation. Tool calls now settle deterministically. The model faked success. On tasks it could not do (opening another website, for example) the base model substituted a tool it did have and reported success 84% of the time. I trained an adapter that teaches it to name what it cannot do instead, which also makes its WebMCP tool-call decisions better. Accomplishments that we're proud of The privacy layer works end to end. An outside agent asked for the gist of my notes and got a summary computed on my GPU, in seconds, without ever seeing the notes. An adapter that makes the agent honest. False success on impossible tasks went from 84% to 0%. Live, on the same task, the base model substitutes the site's own search for the website it cannot open and reports on that instead; with the adapter it answers "I cannot open Google or any other site" in under half a minute, without a single click. In a longer rehearsal the base model went further: eleven typing attempts into a dead field over five minutes. One request, one call. Asked to turn a private note into a story, the agent did not click its way through the app: it made one tool call and a finished five-slide story appeared, title and all. One page, every tool. An agent on one Mentria tab can use the tools of every other open tab, through one standard interface. An agent that tests the site. The same on-device model QA-tests Mentria's own tools and reports what it finds, so agents are first-class users here in more than one sense. What we learned A real model you own, that can operate real tools, is a better product than 34 tools or "privacy" alone, and a web standard is what lets outside agents join that same surface without a server in the loop. Agents are first-class users: testing with them finds bugs humans never trigger. For tool-using agents, honesty about which tools exist beats cleverness; that is what the adapter really taught. And a local model is not just a feature, it is the place to put the parts of a task that should never leave the device. What's next for Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI The privacy layer grows from summaries to actions: a cloud agent filling in an invoice can ask the local model for the details that live in a locked note, and once you have unlocked it, the local model answers with only the fields needed, no copy-paste and no human in the loop for every step. Beyond that, a single conversational surface for all the AI tools, and an Extension Studio where the on-device model writes single-file apps that compose these capabilities instead of rewriting them, so anyone can grow the toolbox in a sentence. Provenance and the judged build: the site predates the challenge; everything WebMCP above was built during the submission window (commits from 2026-09-01, listed in WEBMCP.md). MIT licensed. Submitted as a frozen snapshot: webmcp.mentria.ai and the webmcp-demo repo hold the exact judged build and will not change during judging; production continues at mentria.ai (main repo github.com/mentria-ai/website, tag webmcp-submission ).
